Operations / Q4 2026

Q4 2026
Operations Playbook

Prepared for: Delivery, Support, and Operations teams
Owner: Dave John Deluta  |  Version: 1.0  |  Review date: 06 November 2026

Purpose. This playbook turns the Q4 operating plan into a practical weekly rhythm: protect customer commitments, surface risk early, and make handoffs clear enough that work continues without a single point of failure.

What success looks like

  • Committed work is visible, sequenced, and owned.
  • Customer-impacting risks are raised before they become incidents.
  • Every completed initiative leaves behind a decision record and a named follow-up owner.

Quarter priorities

  1. Improve delivery predictability through smaller release slices.
  2. Reduce repeat support issues with durable documentation and enablement.
  3. Close the year with clean operational metrics and a ready Q1 backlog.

Internal working document. Use the latest approved version in the shared workspace when making commitments.

1. Operating Model

The team operates as one delivery system. Product intent, implementation detail, customer context, and operational readiness are reviewed together rather than passed between disconnected queues.

Decision principles

  • Make the next decision reversible. Prefer small experiments when the cost of waiting is low.
  • Escalate with evidence. Bring the observed impact, the affected commitment, and a recommended next step.
  • Write it down once. The decision log is the source of truth for scope, trade-offs, and follow-up.
  • Leave the system easier to run. Every release should improve a runbook, alert, test, or customer-facing explanation.

Core roles

RolePrimary accountabilityBackup
Delivery leadSequence work, manage commitments, facilitate risk review.Operations lead
Operations leadReadiness, incident coordination, service health, handoff quality.Delivery lead
Customer partnerFeedback themes, expectation setting, acceptance signals.Account owner
Technical ownerImplementation quality, dependencies, rollback and verification plan.Designated reviewer

Working agreements

Default to async updates before meetings. Meetings end with an owner, a due date, and a written decision. If a commitment changes, update the plan and notify affected partners the same day.

2. Weekly Cadence

The weekly cadence is deliberately repetitive. Predictable checkpoints reduce coordination overhead and give risks several opportunities to be corrected before Friday.

WhenCheckpointExpected output
Monday AMCommitment reviewTop outcomes, owners, dependencies, and confidence for the week.
Tuesday PMDelivery clinicBlocked work receives a decision, pairing session, or explicit escalation.
WednesdayCustomer signal reviewSupport themes and feedback translated into actions or backlog items.
Thursday PMRelease readinessGo/no-go decision, rollback owner, monitoring checks, and comms draft.
FridayCloseout and learningCompleted outcomes, carryover rationale, metrics, and one improvement experiment.

Monday commitment checklist

  • Confirm the three most important outcomes, not a long task inventory.
  • Mark each outcome green, amber, or red with one sentence of evidence.
  • Identify work that depends on another team or an unavailable decision.
  • Reserve capacity for support, defects, and operational interrupts.

Friday closeout prompts

What changed for customers? What did we learn? Which risk moved? What should be stopped, started, or simplified next week?

3. Delivery Controls

Delivery controls keep scope and quality visible without turning the team into a reporting function. Use the lightest control that makes the risk obvious.

Readiness gate

ControlEvidence requiredOwner
ScopeAcceptance criteria and exclusions are agreed.Delivery lead
QualityTest evidence, known limitations, and review completed.Technical owner
OperationsMonitoring, support note, rollback path, and ownership confirmed.Operations lead
CustomerAudience, timing, and message are approved.Customer partner

Risk register fields

  • Risk: a specific uncertain event, not a general concern.
  • Trigger: the observable signal that changes the response.
  • Impact: customer, delivery, financial, or operational consequence.
  • Response: mitigation, contingency, and decision owner.
  • Review date: when the risk must be actively reconsidered.
Rule of thumb: an amber item without a next action is only a status color. Convert it into a dated decision or remove the amber label.

Change control

Changes to a committed outcome require a short note covering the reason, impact, alternatives considered, and the new expectation. Keep the original commitment visible so the learning is not lost.

4. Support and Escalation

Support signals are operational data. Classify them consistently, respond proportionally, and use recurring themes to improve the product and the runbook.

Escalation matrix

SeverityExampleInitial responseUpdate rhythm
S1 — CriticalBroad outage or data integrity concern.Page operations lead immediately; establish incident channel.Every 30 minutes
S2 — HighMaterial customer impact with workaround unavailable.Assign incident owner and customer communicator.Every 2 hours
S3 — NormalDegraded workflow or repeatable defect.Queue with evidence and target date.Daily while active
S4 — LowQuestion, idea, or cosmetic issue.Document answer or add to backlog.At next review

Incident minimums

  • Name one incident lead and one communications owner.
  • Record the timeline as facts, not guesses.
  • State the current customer impact in every update.
  • Close with a follow-up list, owners, and dates.

Support review

Each Wednesday, group incoming issues by theme and frequency. Select one repeat theme for a durable fix, improved documentation, or a customer education action.

5. Templates and Checklists

Use these short formats to keep recurring work consistent. Copy the structure, then add only the context needed for the decision at hand.

Weekly update

Outcome: What changed this week?
Confidence: Green / amber / red, with evidence.
Risk: What might change the commitment?
Ask: What decision or help is needed, and by when?

Decision record

FieldPrompt
ContextWhat problem or opportunity made this decision necessary?
DecisionWhat will we do now?
AlternativesWhat options were considered and why were they not selected?
ReviewWhat signal would cause us to revisit this decision?

Before you close an item

  • Link the outcome to the original commitment.
  • Record known limitations and follow-up work.
  • Confirm the receiving owner understands the next action.
  • Update the customer-facing explanation if expectations changed.

5. Q4 Handoff and Q1 Readiness

A strong quarter ends with transfer of context, not just a final status report. The Q1 team should be able to understand what was delivered, what remains uncertain, and where to start.

Handoff checklist

  1. Archive final decisions, release notes, and customer communications.
  2. Confirm owners for open risks, recurring support themes, and scheduled work.
  3. Review dashboards, alerts, access, and runbooks with the incoming owner.
  4. Convert unresolved questions into explicit Q1 backlog items.
  5. Capture the quarter’s three most useful operating lessons.

Q4 review scorecard

MeasureTargetReview question
Commitment confidenceImproving week over weekAre estimates becoming more reliable?
Escalation lead timeSame business dayDo risks reach the right owner early?
Repeat issue rateDownward trendAre fixes removing causes, not symptoms?
Handoff completeness100% of active items ownedCan Q1 start without rediscovery?
Closing note. Operational maturity is the ability to make good work repeatable. Keep the cadence, make the evidence visible, and improve one control at a time.
